concepts.title: Monohybrid Cross Ratios and the Test Cross
concepts.definition: Crossing pure tall with pure dwarf peas hides the dwarf allele in an all-tall F1 of heterozygotes, and selfing that F1 re-reveals the hidden trait in a three-to-one phenotypic split with a one-two-one genotypic split; mating a dominant-looking plant to a recessive one - the test cross - then betrays its genotype, since half-and-half progeny unmask a heterozygote while all-tall progeny prove homozygosity.
concepts.key_idea: Expect three quarters dominant in F2, and read an unknown genotype by crossing to the recessive parent.
question_patterns: in an F2 of 120 pea plants how many are expected tall and how many dwarf
state the phenotypic and genotypic ratios of a monohybrid cross in the F2 generation
a tall pea plant crossed with a dwarf gives half tall and half dwarf progeny - what is its genotype
construct a Punnett square for the selfing of Tt plants and derive the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio
state the law of segregation with the monohybrid cross as evidence
why did the dwarf trait vanish in F1 and reappear in F2

solution_steps.explain: Three of every four F2 plants show the dominant trait.
Whatever is left of the progeny expresses the recessive trait.

worked_examples.q: What phenotypic ratio does the F2 of a monohybrid cross show: 3:1 or 9:3:3:1?

concepts.title: Incomplete Dominance and Codominance in Flowers
concepts.definition: Not every allele pair obeys boss-and-hidden rules: in the four-o'clock plant red crossed with white gives pink F1 hybrids and a one-two-one red-pink-white F2, because each allele is only partly expressed, while in cattle coats and the MN blood group both alleles speak at once - roan animals and MN red cells - which is codominance.
concepts.key_idea: Half of the F2 is the blend class under incomplete dominance, and half of that is the pure recessive class.
question_patterns: cross red Mirabilis with white - give the F1 colour and the F2 phenotypic ratio with counts for 80 plants
differentiate incomplete dominance from codominance with one plant and one animal example
why does the roan coat of cattle show both red and white hairs
write the genotype and antigen pattern of the three MN blood groups
how many pink-flowered plants appear among 60 F2 progeny of a pink selfing
which ratio distinguishes incomplete dominance from a normal dominant-recessive F2

solution_steps.explain: Heterozygotes show the intermediate phenotype, half of the F2.

solution_steps.action: halve again for a pure class
solution_steps.explain: The 1:2:1 split makes each homozygous class half the heterozygote class.

worked_examples.q: Red crossed with white in the four-o'clock plant gives what colour F1: pink or red?

concepts.title: Dihybrid Cross and Independent Assortment
concepts.definition: Following two traits at once - round versus wrinkled seeds, yellow versus green - Mendel saw all round-yellow F1 plants and, on selfing, a nine-three-three-one F2 spread across sixteen genotypic squares, with fresh trait pairings appearing; this independence of allele pairs became his law of independent assortment.
concepts.key_idea: Nine sixteenths carry both dominants, three sixteenths carry exactly one, and one sixteenth carries both recessives.
question_patterns: out of 320 F2 seeds of a dihybrid cross how many are round yellow wrinkled yellow round green and wrinkled green
state the law of independent assortment with the dihybrid cross as its evidence
which two new trait combinations appear in the F2 of RRYY crossed with rryy that are absent in the parents
derive the 9:3:3:1 ratio from the sixteen boxes of the dihybrid Punnett square
how many F2 genotypic classes does a dihybrid cross produce
a dihybrid yields 96 offspring - how many show both recessive traits

solution_steps.explain: Nine of the sixteen squares combine both dominant traits.
Only one square carries both recessive traits.

worked_examples.q: What F2 ratio does a dihybrid cross give: 9:3:3:1 or 3:1?

concepts.title: Linkage, Crossing Over and Map Distance
concepts.definition: Genes seated on one chromosome travel together as a linkage group, so Bateson and Punnett's sweet pea and Morgan's flies broke the 9:3:3:1 expectation; only an exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids - crossing over - lets parental combinations loosen, and the recombinant share of progeny doubles as the chromosome map distance, one percent of recombinants marking one centimorgan.
concepts.key_idea: Add the parental classes, subtract from a hundred, and the remainder prices the recombination and the map distance.
question_patterns: Morgan's test cross gave 41.5 percent grey vestigial and 41.5 percent black long flies - find the parental and recombinant percentages
why did the sweet pea cross of Bateson and Punnett deviate from the 9:3:3:1 ratio
define linkage and name the scientist who explained it in Drosophila
what is a centimorgan and how is it fixed from recombinant frequency
how did Creighton and McClintock prove crossing over with maize chromosome 9
distinguish parental from non-parental combinations in a test cross progeny

solution_steps.explain: The two most frequent classes keep the parental trait pairing.
The remainder carries the exchanged, non-parental combinations.

worked_examples.q: One percent of recombinants marks what map distance: one centimorgan or one metre?

concepts.title: Sex-linked Inheritance in Drosophila
concepts.definition: Morgan's stray white-eyed male revealed that eye colour rides the X chromosome: red-to-white crosses hide the trait in red F1 flies, yet F2 white eyes appear only in males, because a male's single X carries no partner to mask the recessive; colour blindness and haemophilia follow the same X-linked route in humans.
concepts.key_idea: Half the sons of a carrier mother inherit the affected X, so the disorder lands on half of the male progeny.
question_patterns: a carrier red-eyed female Drosophila mates a red-eyed male - what fraction of the sons will be white-eyed
why did all white-eyed flies in Morgan's F2 turn out to be male
explain why haemophilia shows up mostly in males of the British royal family
write the genotypes of the F1 from a white-eyed male crossed with a pure red-eyed female
name two sex-linked disorders of humans and the chromosome that carries them
what fraction of the daughters of a carrier mother are carriers themselves

solution_steps.explain: Half of all offspring are sons.
A carrier mother passes the affected X to half of her sons.

worked_examples.q: Morgan's stray white-eyed fly was which sex: male or female?

concepts.title: Extrachromosomal Maternal Inheritance
concepts.definition: Plastids and mitochondria carry their own DNA, and because the sperm sheds its cytoplasm at fertilisation, these organellar genomes pass down the maternal line alone; the white, green and variegated leaves of the four-o'clock plant demonstrated that cytoplasmic traits follow the mother's phenotype rather than Mendel's rules.
concepts.key_idea: No paternal contribution reaches plastids or mitochondria, so offspring mirror the mother's cytoplasmic genotype.
question_patterns: why do plastid and mitochondrial genomes show maternal inheritance
explain the variegated leaf phenotype of the four-o'clock plant through plastid genes
what happens to the sperm cytoplasm before fertilisation and why does it matter
differentiate cytoplasmic inheritance from nuclear Mendelian inheritance
what did the reciprocal crosses of green white and variegated four-o'clock plants show
name two cell organelles that carry DNA outside the chromosomes

solution_steps.explain: Traits coded by plastid or mitochondrial DNA fall outside Mendelian segregation.
Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg, so organellar genomes come solely from the mother.
Progeny phenotype matches the female parent's leaf type - maternal or uniparental inheritance.

worked_examples.q: Plastids and mitochondria pass down which parent's line: the mother's or the father's?

concepts.title: Polyploidy Levels and Chromosome Sets
concepts.definition: Ploidy counts complete chromosome sets: rice with two sets, peanuts and cotton with four, bread wheat with six and strawberry or sugarcane with eight; multiply the chromosomes of one set by the ploidy level to get the somatic total, and over thirty percent of plant species exploit such polyploidy for larger organs and tougher field performance.
concepts.key_idea: One set times the ploidy level sizes the genome; halving the total gives what a gamete must carry.
question_patterns: wheat carries 7 chromosomes per set and is hexaploid - compute its total chromosome number
a plant has 10 chromosomes in one set and 80 in total - find its ploidy level
how many chromosomes does a gamete of sugarcane carry if the plant is octoploid with 10 per set
differentiate triploid tetraploid hexaploid and octoploid with one plant example of each
why is polyploidy common in plants but rare in animals
what is aneuploidy and which meiotic fault produces it

solution_steps.explain: Each complete set holds the base number of chromosomes.
Meiosis distributes one chromosome of each pair, half the somatic total.

worked_examples.q: Bread wheat carries how many sets of chromosomes: six or sixty?

concepts.title: Forward and Reverse Genetics
concepts.definition: Two research directions bracket the gene: forward genetics starts from visible or molecular phenotypic variation and hunts for the DNA behind it, while reverse genetics begins with a sequenced gene or protein of unknown job, silences or disrupts it - say by RNA interference - and reads the resulting phenotype to deduce its function.
concepts.key_idea: Phenotype-to-gene is forward; gene-to-phenotype is reverse, with RNAi or targeted disruption as the probe.
question_patterns: differentiate the forward and reverse genetics approaches with a diagram of each direction
which small double stranded molecules does RNA interference deploy and against what target
why can reverse genetics characterise genes that show no visible variation
what is a candidate gene and how is its function tested in a reverse approach
how did genome sequencing change the balance between forward and reverse genetics
name two techniques used to disrupt or silence a chosen gene

solution_steps.explain: Phenotypic variation first means forward; DNA or protein sequence first means reverse.
Forward screens mutants; reverse silences or disrupts a candidate gene, often through RNAi or homologous recombination.
The change in organism development reveals what the disrupted gene normally does.

worked_examples.q: Starting from a phenotype and hunting the gene is which genetics: forward or reverse?
